If you need automated report distribution, start by matching the feature set to cost, not brand.

Imagine a company with Azure SQL,
and Power BI Pro dashboards.
They lack automation and subscription capabilities.
In the past they used SSRS or Crystal Reports.

SSRS can generate paginated reports and supports dynamic subscriptions.
But it requires a SQL Server license that can cost $8 k per core,
and Microsoft is de‑prioritising SSRS.
You would be paying for a product that may not get new features.

Power BI Paginated Reports run on the Power BI service.
You can start with a modest Fabric capacity (F2) for a few thousand dollars a year.
If demand spikes you scale to a larger node (F4) and still stay below the two‑year cost of a SQL Server license.
This also gives you immediate access to the rest of the Fabric ecosystem.

For most teams, moving to Power BI Paginated Reports on Fabric provides the needed automation,
lower upfront cost,
and a future‑proof path.
Only consider SSRS if you already own a SQL Server license and have heavy on‑premises dependencies.

Evaluate the total cost of ownership and the roadmap of the tools before you commit.
Choose the option that lets you deliver reports today without locking yourself into a legacy product.

news_posts.post_content:
Imagine you need to run a similarity search over product descriptions for a recommendation engine.
Your current pipeline moves the text into a dedicated vector store,
adds latency,
and requires extra ops work.
Now picture the same query running straight inside PostgreSQL,
using the new pg_vectorsearch extension.
The contrast is clear – you keep data in one place and avoid the sync hassle.

Tiger Data just open‑sourced pg_vectorsearch.
It adds vector indexes and similarity operators right to the core engine.
No need to spin up a separate service or learn a new query language.
You write standard SQL,
store embeddings in a column,
and let the extension handle the nearest‑neighbor search.

For data engineers this means fewer moving parts and lower maintenance overhead.
It also simplifies security reviews because everything stays inside the database.
If you already use PostgreSQL, try creating a vector column,
load a few embeddings,
and run a simple SELECT … ORDER BY vector <-> query_vector LIMIT 5.
You’ll see how close the results feel compared to a specialized vector DB.

The practical takeaway is to evaluate pg_vectorsearch when you need vector search but want to stay within your existing relational stack.

news_posts.post_content:
When IT teams drown in repetitive tickets
service quality suffers.
A simple way to break that cycle is to let an AI agent handle routine queries.
Cielo did exactly that.
It deployed a Microsoft‑built AI assistant that cut its ticket volume by more than half
according to Microsoft.
The idea is to use the AI as a first‑line triage that matches user requests to documented solutions.
This works best when the knowledge base is structured and kept up to date.
Here is a quick checklist you can apply today.
Identify the top five recurring issues in your ticket logs.
Gather the official resolution steps for each issue in a searchable format.
Choose an LLM that supports retrieval‑augmented generation or fine‑tuning.
Connect the model to your ticketing platform so it can suggest answers or close tickets automatically.
Track metrics such as ticket count, first‑response time, and false‑positive closures.
Fact: Cielo reduced tickets by more than 50 % after the AI agent went live.
Interpretation: Similar gains are realistic if you start small, automate only well‑defined queries, and monitor performance.
Recommendation: Map your top ticket categories and pilot an AI bot on a single category before scaling.

concept_posts.post_content:
Example: A data pipeline processes 2 TB of logs each night on a cloud data warehouse.
The job runs on a large,
 on‑demand compute cluster and costs $500 per run.
The team sees the monthly bill rise above expectations.
Instead of leaving it as‑is,
 they look at three simple levers.

- Choose spot or preemptible instances for non‑critical stages.
 This can cut compute spend by 60 % or more.
- Enable auto‑scaling and set idle timeouts.
 This reduces idle cost dramatically.
- Partition and prune data early.
 Smaller scans mean less processing time and lower storage I/O charges.

A common mistake is to over‑provision resources based on peak load and never adjust them.
That creates a constant drag on the budget.

Rule of thumb: Review usage metrics weekly and right‑size any component that sits below 30 % utilization for three consecutive days.
What steps will you take to trim cloud data costs in your next sprint?

Many people enable Row-Level Security and then forget to attach any policy,
leaving the table completely locked for everyone.
This simple oversight turns a security feature into a denial‑of‑service for your own users.

Here is a quick checklist you can run after you create a policy.

Example: a sales table where each rep should only see rows that belong to them.
You create a policy that filters on the rep_id column.

- Define the policy with a USING clause that references the correct column,
and test it with a role that mimics the end‑user.
- Grant the role the SELECT privilege on the table,
otherwise the policy never gets evaluated.
- Verify the policy works by connecting as the role and running a simple SELECT,
checking that only the expected rows appear.

Common mistake to avoid: using a static value in the USING clause, such as rep_id = 1,
which gives every user the same view.

Rule of thumb: always validate a new RLS policy with a low‑privilege role before rolling it out to production.
